newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see burst in biotech profitability.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see burst in biotech profitability.

text.p: While extreme stock price volatility and steep losses in the biotech industry have kept many investors away, the sector is poised for a burst of profitability over the next five years, analysts told the Montgomery Securities Investment Conference.
In fact, the biotech industry is using R&D capital more effectively than the pharmaceutical sector to develop New Chemical Entities (NCEs), Montgomery analyst Scott Sacane said.
He forecast the number of profitable biotech companies would jump to 35 or more by the year 2002.
By comparison, there were no profitable biotech companies as recently as 1986, and there are expected to be six in the black at the end of this year.

Along with value being created through new drug approvals, Sacane predicted biotech companies will increasingly become acquisition targets of pharmaceutical companies looking to fill a near term gap in their own new drug development.
An increasing share of the NCEs being approved, he said, is coming out of the biotech sector. In 1985 there was one biotech NCE approval, compared with 29 non-biotech.
That shifted to seven biotech and 21 non-biotech last year, and Sacane forecast the mix in 2002 would be 16 biotech NCE approvals, versus 20 non-biotech.

He stressed the pharmaceutical NCE approval rate is flat despite increasing R&D spending, and said several of these comanies will find it more cost effective to acquire a biotech comany than to step up internal R&D spending sufficiently to boost the level of product approval.
"There is going to be a dramatic increase in outsourcing by pharmaceutical companies," Sacane said.

But another Montgomery analyst, David Crossen, cautioned there were still reasons for concern. A key issue, he said, is whether the U.S. Food and Drug Administation could triple its rate of drug approval to avoid a huge backlog as the number of biotech drug candidates explodes.
Moreover, he said, the FDA's emphasis on rapid approval for drugs to treat cancer, HIV and AIDS, and to improve mortality rates in various illnesses could be a concern for other drug categories.
"They're getting certain drugs out more quickly, but where does that leave the others?" Crossen asked.

He also said that with some 1,200 biotech drugs currently in development, competition in the industry will become far more fierce and that companes and investors will need to become more vigilant in anticipating competitive threats.
